title: System Design — Scale from zero to millions

questions.question: Why separate web/mobile traffic servers from database servers early?
options: So DNS stops resolving and users cannot find the site anymore.
So web tier and data tier can be scaled independently as load grows.
So you can delete the database and keep only static HTML forever.
So mobile apps are forced to speak FTP instead of HTTP in real production systems at scale.
questions.explanation: Separating web/mobile traffic (web tier) and database (data tier) servers allows them to be scaled independently

reference.book: System Design Interview – An Insider's Guide
reference.excerpt: Separating web/mobile traffic (web tier) and database (data tier) servers allows them to be scaled independently

questions.question: Vertical scaling (“scale up”) means:
options: Adding more servers into a pool of identical machines in real production systems at scale.
Adding more power (CPU, RAM, etc.) to your existing servers.
Removing all CPUs so the system uses less electricity overnight.
Sharding every table on day one with ten users total in real production systems at scale.
questions.explanation: Vertical scaling, referred to as “scale up”, means the process of adding more power (CPU, RAM, etc.) to your servers

reference.book: System Design Interview – An Insider's Guide
reference.excerpt: Vertical scaling, referred to as “scale up”, means the process of adding more power (CPU, RAM, etc.) to your servers

questions.question: A hard limitation of vertical scaling alone is:
options: It always provides automatic multi-server failover and redundancy in real production systems at scale.
You cannot add unlimited CPU/memory to one machine, and one failure takes the site down.
It is illegal in every cloud provider’s terms of service worldwide in real production systems at scale.
It only works for mobile apps and never for web browsers in real production systems at scale.
questions.explanation: Vertical scaling has a hard limit… Vertical scaling does not have failover and redundancy

reference.book: System Design Interview – An Insider's Guide
reference.excerpt: Vertical scaling has a hard limit… Vertical scaling does not have failover and redundancy

questions.question: For most developers, Xu says relational databases are often best first because:
options: Joins are illegal in SQL and must be avoided at all costs forever in real production systems at scale.
They have decades of history and have historically worked well for many apps.
They never store tables or rows and only store graphs in real production systems at scale.
They always beat every NoSQL store on every latency benchmark in real production systems at scale.
questions.explanation: For most developers, relational databases are the best option because they have been around for over 40 years

reference.book: System Design Interview – An Insider's Guide
reference.excerpt: For most developers, relational databases are the best option because they have been around for over 40 years

questions.question: NoSQL may be worth exploring when, among other reasons:
options: You need joins across every table on every request without exception in real production systems at scale.
You need super-low latency, unstructured data, simple serialize/deserialize, or massive scale.
Your only requirement is ACID transactions with heavy multi-table joins in real production systems at scale.
You want to ban JSON and only store handwritten paper forms in real production systems at scale.
questions.explanation: Non-relational databases might be the right choice if: … super-low latency … unstructured … serialize and deserialize … massive amount of data

reference.book: System Design Interview – An Insider's Guide
reference.excerpt: Non-relational databases might be the right choice if: … super-low latency … unstructured … serialize and deserialize … massive amount of data

questions.question: True or false: Horizontal scaling adds more servers to your resource pool (“scale-out”).
questions.explanation: Horizontal scaling, referred to as “scale-out”, allows you to scale by adding more servers into your pool of resources

reference.book: System Design Interview – An Insider's Guide
reference.excerpt: Horizontal scaling, referred to as “scale-out”, allows you to scale by adding more servers into your pool of resources

questions.question: A CDN is primarily used to:
options: Replace your transactional database for all strongly consistent writes.
Serve static content from locations closer to users to cut latency.
Run all business logic inside the user’s DNS resolver process in real production systems at scale.
Guarantee exactly-once delivery of every database transaction in real production systems at scale.

reference.book: System Design Interview – An Insider's Guide

questions.question: Message queues help large systems mainly by:
options: Forcing every request to wait synchronously on the slowest downstream forever.
Decoupling producers and consumers so work can be processed asynchronously.
Deleting failed jobs so operators never see errors in dashboards in real production systems at scale.
Replacing TLS so all traffic stays unencrypted for speed in real production systems at scale.

reference.book: System Design Interview – An Insider's Guide
